title: Jallianwala Bagh, Vaisakhi 1919
hookLine: British troops fire on an unarmed crowd in a walled garden in Amritsar, killing hundreds

lines: A GARDEN NEAR THE GOLDEN TEMPLE.
cards: Vaisakhi afternoon, 1919, in Amritsar. Thousands of people sit on the grass in a public garden a few minutes' walk from the Golden Temple. Vaisakhi is the spring harvest festival, and for Sikhs the birthday of the Khalsa.
The city is full: families in from the villages, bright turbans and scarves, a visit to the Harmandir, food, music, fairs. Some in the garden have come to hear speeches.
Many have just come in from the festival to sit down.

teach.b: Jallianwala Bagh was open ground in the middle of the city, closed in on all sides by the walls of houses, with only a few narrow ways in and out. That spring, Punjab was tense.
There had been protests against new British laws allowing arrest without trial; two popular local leaders, one Hindu and one Muslim, had been arrested; public meetings had been banned.
Many in the garden, especially the visitors from villages, likely didn't know about the ban. The crowd was Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together, and it was unarmed.

teach.h: AN UNARMED CROWD, FIRED ON WITHOUT WARNING.
teach.b: A British officer, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer, arrived with troops, stationed them at the main entrance, and without any warning ordered them to fire into the crowd.
The firing went on for about ten minutes, until the ammunition was nearly spent. People tried to climb the walls. Some jumped into a well to escape.
The official British count was 379 killed; Indian estimates were far higher, around a thousand. Many more were wounded. Nobody knows the true number.
The massacre shocked India and many in Britain.
The poet Rabindranath Tagore gave back his knighthood in protest, and that afternoon is often described as a turning point on the road to Indian independence.
The garden is a memorial now, with bullet marks still in the walls and the well.
And Amritsar's spring festival carries a second memory: each Vaisakhi, people gather in the garden to remember that afternoon.

how: The Jallianwala Bagh is a national memorial in Amritsar, near Harmandir Sahib; each year on 13 April, Vaisakhi, people gather there to remember those killed, and many Sikhs include them in their Vaisakhi remembrance.

games.q: you're a villager in Amritsar for Vaisakhi, 1919. you've visited the Harmandir. what are you most likely doing that afternoon?
o: sitting in a public garden, perhaps unaware of a ban on meetings.
games.why: many in the crowd had come in from the festival and likely didn't know of the ban. the crowd was unarmed.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it; if not, picture one, a small steady flame. Let it stand for the people in the garden that afternoon, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, who came for a festival and didn't go home.
You don't need to picture what happened: just watch the flame, let it be their light, and if you pray, hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Jallianwala Bagh. The walled garden in Amritsar where, on Vaisakhi in 1919, British troops fired on an unarmed crowd, killing hundreds.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bagh, a garden, a word from Persian.

carryVoice: Your line: vaisakhi, remembered. A festival day that now holds a second memory. That's day two hundred ninety-seven.
